summary: This RFC describes how Internet mail systems route messages using information from the domain system, in particular how mailers interpret MX records. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 2821.

eli5.summary: When mail arrives for a name, the mail system looks up which computer takes mail for it, using a special entry in the naming system.

questions: how do mx records route mail
how does mail routing work with dns
how does a mailer choose which mx to try
subtitle: How a mail server uses DNS MX records to decide where to deliver a message.

tldr.problem: Once domain names arrived, a mailer could no longer just open a connection to the host in the address, because the domain system might point mail somewhere else or offer several routes.
tldr.mechanism: The mailer asks for MX records, which hold a preference number and a host name, discards unsuitable ones and tries the rest from lowest preference upward.
tldr.outcome: It is Historic and was replaced by RFC 2821.

today: RFC 974 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 2821.

sections.title: Why Mail Routing Changed
sections.content:
The memo explains how mailers decide how to route a message addressed to an Internet domain name, by interpreting MX resource records. It says nothing about MB and MG records, which are for mailbox names.

Before domains, a mailer could usually open an SMTP connection to the host in the address, with special cases in configuration files for hosts such as UUCP and CSNET ones. Under domains, the mailer must ask the domain system where mail for a name goes. The answer may be an entirely different host, or a choice of routes.
sections.eli5: You used to mail a letter straight to a house. Now you first ask the post office which house really takes mail for that name.

sections.title: MX Records
sections.content:
Domain servers store information as resource records (RRs). An MX RR pairs a domain name with a preference value (an unsigned 16-bit integer) and the name of a host. The lowest-numbered MX is tried first, and several MXs with the same preference have the same priority.

Mailers may also meet the CNAME RR, which says a name is an alias for a canonical name, and the Well Known Service (WKS) RR, which records the services such as SMTP that a name supports.
sections.eli5: An MX entry says who takes mail for a name and gives a ranking number. The smallest number is the first choice.

sections.title: Querying and Choosing Hosts
sections.content:
The mailer on LOCAL first queries for MX RRs for REMOTE, and the RFC strongly urges doing so every time it sends. No response, a response with the truncation bit set, or a non-zero response code are errors. A truncated answer must not be used and the query should be repeated over a virtual circuit. A CNAME answer means the query is repeated with the canonical name.

If the MX list is empty, the mailer treats it as one MX with preference 0 and the host REMOTE, and delivers there. Otherwise it may discard MX hosts whose WKS record shows no mail service (optional but strongly encouraged), and it must discard every MX whose preference is greater than or equal to LOCAL's own, if LOCAL is listed. This prevents mail loops.

The mailer is required to try the lowest-valued MX and is encouraged to continue in order until one accepts. All MXs sharing a preference must be tried before any higher one.
sections.eli5: Ask who takes the mail, cross off any computers that cannot or should not, then try the smallest number first and work upward.

sections.title: Loops, Caches and Special Cases
sections.content:
Out-of-date information is a looping risk because resolver caches only learn of table changes when they time out. The RFC rejects forcing queries to authoritative servers as impractical, and instead advises checking with a host's administrator before adding it as an MX. Answers with incomplete answer sections must not be accepted.

Wildcard records such as *.IL can route a whole domain through a relay like RELAY.CS.NET; domain servers hide the wildcard, and a mailer receiving a wildcard name in an RR should discard it. Aliases should never be used in MX data. MX processing is done only for REMOTE and is not repeated for the MX hosts, so chains of MXs do not work.
sections.eli5: Old phone-book copies can send mail the wrong way, so people must be careful when changing entries. A relay is a helper who takes mail for a whole region.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content: The RFC uses a database of four hosts, A to D at EXAMPLE.ORG. A has MXs at preference 10 (itself), 15 (B) and 20 (C). A mailer on D sending to A keeps all three and must try A first. A mailer on B sending to A must discard B and C, because B's own preference is 15 and the RFC discards every MX at or above the local one, leaving only A. A mailer on A sending to D sees two MXs with preference 0 (D and C) and may try either first.
sections.eli5: The examples show a mailer crossing off candidates that rank at or below itself, then trying the best one left.

items.label: Mail exchanger
items.desc: Preference value plus host name; lowest is tried first.

items.label: Canonical name
items.desc: The queried name is an alias for another name.

items.label: Well Known Service
items.desc: Which network services, such as SMTP, a name supports.
